pos: v. and adj. (past participle of drink; overcome with strong drink)
etymology: Past participle of drink, Saxon drincan. The Authorized Version uses the word both innocently — men who have eaten and drunk — and morally, and it is one of the few sins Scripture illustrates chiefly by showing what it did to particular men on particular nights.
biblical_def: “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). Paul sets the two fillings against each other, and the contrast tells us what drunkenness actually is: a man surrendering the governance of himself to something, and the question is only to what. Scripture then shows the ruin in cases. David “made him drunk” (2Sa 11:13) — the king could not get Uriah to go down to his own house sober, so he tried it with wine, and when even a drunk Uriah kept faith with the ark and the army in the field, David wrote the letter. Elah was “drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza” when Zimri killed him (1Ki 16:9); Benhadad and thirty-two kings were “drinking themselves drunk in the pavilions” at noon on the day their army was broken (1Ki 20:16). Belshazzar drank wine out of the vessels of the LORD's house and praised gods of silver and gold, and the hand wrote on the wall that night (Dan 5:23). The word also carries the wrath of God in a fearful figure: “I will make mine arrows drunk with blood” (Deu 32:42), and Jerusalem “hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury” (Isa 51:17) — the cup our Lord took at Gethsemane and drained.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines drunk as intoxicated, inebriated; and adds the Scriptural sense of being drenched or saturated — as arrows made drunk with blood.
webster_full: DRUNK, a. Intoxicated; inebriated with strong liquor.
1. Drenched or saturated with moisture or liquor. I will make my arrows drunk with blood. Deuteronomy 32.
DRUNKENNESS, n. Intoxication; inebriation; a state in which a person is overwhelmed or overpowered with spirituous liquors.
2. Disorder of the faculties resembling intoxication by liquors; inflammation; frenzy; rage.
scriptures: Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
And when David had called him, he did eat and drink before him; and he made him drunk: and at even he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord, but went not down to his house.
Dan 5:23

But hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before thee, and thou, and thy lords, thy wives, and thy concubines, have drunk wine in them; and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which see not, nor hear, nor know: and the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified:
Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out.
corruption_summary: Drunkenness has been reclassified as a disease and thereby moved out of the category Scripture puts it in.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern account treats drunkenness as an illness with a sufferer rather than a sin with a sinner, and the pastoral consequence is that repentance is no longer the remedy offered. Scripture is not naive about bondage — it says plainly that whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin, and the misery of the habitual drunkard is real and deep. But 1 Corinthians 6:10 lists drunkards among those who shall not inherit the kingdom of God, and then adds the sentence that no disease model can supply: and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified. A category that cannot be repented of cannot be forgiven, and a man told he has only a condition has been robbed of the only door out.

The opposite error is the teetotal absolutism that treats wine itself as evil, which Scripture will not support: it gives wine to make glad the heart of man, our Lord made it at Cana, and Paul told Timothy to use a little for his stomach's sake. The line the Bible draws is not at the cup but at the surrender — wherein is excess. A believer may abstain wholly, and there is much wisdom in it where a conscience is weak or a brother is stumbled; but he abstains as a matter of liberty and love, not because Scripture has forbidden what it blessed.
roots_summary: Hebrew shakar (H7937), to be or become drunk; shikkor (H7910), a drunkard; Greek methusko (G3182), to be intoxicated; asotia (G810), excess, riot.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakar (H7937) — to drink to the full, to become drunk; 2 Samuel 11:13, Deuteronomy 32:42.
Hebrew shathah (H8354) — to drink; the ordinary verb, morally neutral in itself.
Greek methusko (G3182) — to make drunk, to be intoxicated; Ephesians 5:18, Luke 12:45.
Greek asotia (G810) — unsavedness, riot, excess, dissipation; Ephesians 5:18, the state wine is here said to hold.
Greek pleroo (G4137) — to be filled; the imperative set against being drunk — be being filled with the Spirit.
usage: “Be not drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit” — two governances, one man.
“He made him drunk” — and Uriah still would not go home.
“Drinking himself drunk in the pavilions” — at noon, thirty-two kings.

pos: adj. (disgraceful; bringing shame; in the Authorized Version, of Baal and of a drunkard's exposure)
etymology: From shame, Saxon scamu. In Jeremiah the adjective is a substitute name: Israel's prophets refused to let Baal keep his own title and called him the shameful thing, which is what the Hebrew bosheth does throughout the Old Testament.
biblical_def: “According to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to that shameful thing, even altars to burn incense unto Baal” (Jer 11:13). The prophet will not dignify the idol. He names it the shameful thing and then, in case anyone should miss it, identifies it: Baal. This is a settled Old Testament practice — the Hebrew bosheth, shame, is substituted for the god's name in personal names and in prophecy, so that Ishbosheth means man of shame where the original had Baal in it. Scripture refuses the courtesy of the idol's own vocabulary. The second use is Habakkuk's, and it is a picture of exposure: “Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also… the cup of the LORD'S right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory” (Hab 2:16). The Chaldean who made his neighbours drunk to look on their nakedness is handed the same cup, and the glory he displayed is covered with his own vomit. It is coarse on purpose. Shame in Scripture is not primarily a feeling; it is the objective disgrace of being seen as one is, and it falls at last on everything that was set up in the place of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shameful as disgraceful, raising shame in others; infamous; and shame as a painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt or of doing something which injures reputation.
webster_full: SHAMEFUL, a. That brings shame or disgrace; scandalous; disgraceful; injurious to reputation.
1. Indecent; raising shame in others.
SHAME, n. A painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt, or of having done something which injures reputation.
2. The cause or reason of shame; that which brings reproach.
scriptures: For according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to that shameful thing, even altars to burn incense unto Baal.
Hab 2:16
Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD'S right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory.
corruption_summary: Shame is treated as an injury to be removed; Scripture distinguishes the shame of sin from the false shame of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic culture has made shame itself the enemy — a wound inflicted by others, always to be dissolved, never to be heeded. Scripture keeps a sharper set of distinctions. There is a shame that is simply the truth about a sin, and it is a mercy: Jeremiah's complaint against Judah is that they had lost it entirely, neither could they blush (Jer 6:15). There is a shame that Christ bore and thereby removed, so that whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed (Rom 10:11). And there is a shame that is a snare, when a man is ashamed of Christ or of His words before an adulterous generation. Abolishing the category wholesale destroys the second and third along with the first.

Jeremiah's naming of Baal is worth imitating. The prophets did not adopt the idol's preferred title; they called it the shameful thing and then said whose altar it was. Every age has vocabulary that has been carefully built to make a sin sound like a good, and the church's duty is not to be clever about it but to be plain: to name the thing by what it does and whom it dishonours, while dealing tenderly with the people caught by it.
roots_summary: Hebrew bosheth (H1322), shame — used as a substitute name for Baal; qiqalon (H7022), shameful spewing, disgrace; qalon (H7036), dishonour.
roots_lines: Hebrew bosheth (H1322) — shame; Jeremiah 11:13, that shameful thing — the prophets' deliberate substitute for the name Baal.
Hebrew qiqalon (H7022) — shameful spewing, deep disgrace; Habakkuk 2:16, the only occurrence in Scripture.
Hebrew qalon (H7036) — dishonour, ignominy; Habakkuk 2:16, filled with shame for glory.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; the thing the shame is poured upon.
Greek aischune (G152) — shame, disgrace; Hebrews 12:2, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame.
usage: “That shameful thing, even altars… unto Baal” — the prophet naming it twice.
“Shameful spewing shall be on thy glory” — coarse on purpose.
“Filled with shame for glory” — the exchange the proud always make.

pos: adv. (crookedly; in a manner turned aside from right)
etymology: Latin pervertere, to turn thoroughly aside, from per and vertere, to turn. The picture is of a straight thing bent, which is why the confession that uses this word is always a confession of having gone crooked rather than of having gone wrong by accident.
biblical_def: The great use is the model prayer of the exile in Solomon's dedication: “Yet if they shall bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent, and make supplication unto thee… saying, We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness” (1Ki 8:47). Three verbs, and they are not padding. We have sinned — missed the mark. We have done perversely — twisted what was straight. We have committed wickedness — done it wilfully. Daniel prays that prayer almost word for word in Babylon (Dan 9:5), which is exactly what Solomon had asked for; and it remains the pattern of honest confession, refusing to reduce sin to a single mild category. Shimei uses the word to name his own conduct when the wind changed: “neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem” (2Sa 19:19) — a confession made when David was returning in strength, and its sincerity may be measured accordingly. And Psalm 119 uses it of what others do to the godly: “Let the proud be ashamed; for they dealt perversely with me without a cause: but I will meditate in thy precepts” (Psa 119:78). The answer to being dealt with crookedly is not to bend in return but to meditate in what is straight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perverse as literally turned aside, hence distorted from the right; and perversely as with intent to vex, crossly, stubbornly.
webster_full: PERVERSE, a. Literally, turned aside; hence, distorted from the right.
1. Obstinate in the wrong; disposed to be contrary; stubborn; untractable.
2. Cross; petulant; peevish; disposed to cross and vex.
PERVERSELY, adv. With intent to vex; crossly; peevishly; obstinately in the wrong.
scriptures: Yet if they shall bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent, and make supplication unto thee in the land of them that carried them captives, saying, We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness;
Let the proud be ashamed; for they dealt perversely with me without a cause: but I will meditate in thy precepts.

And said unto the king, Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
corruption_summary: Confession has been reduced to a single soft word; Solomon's prayer uses three, and the middle one is this.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern confession, public and private, tends toward a single mild formula — mistakes were made, we fell short, we are all works in progress. 1 Kings 8:47 gives the exile a threefold confession that refuses every escape: sinned, done perversely, committed wickedness. Missing the mark, twisting what was straight, and doing evil on purpose are three different admissions, and a man who will make only the first has not yet confessed. Daniel, the most blameless man in the book that bears his name, prayed all three in the first person plural and included himself.

The other half of the word belongs to the sufferer. They dealt perversely with me without a cause — and the psalmist's response is to meditate in God's precepts. The natural answer to crooked treatment is crooked treatment, and the whole of Psalm 119 is a man refusing it, going back again and again to the straight rule while the proud bend everything around him. Perverseness is answered by the word, not by returning the twist.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'avah (H5753), to bend, twist, do perversely; 'avon (H5771), iniquity, crookedness; chata' (H2398), to miss the mark, to sin.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'avah (H5753) — to bend, to make crooked, to do perversely; 1 Kings 8:47, 2 Samuel 19:19.
Hebrew 'avon (H5771) — iniquity, guilt, the crookedness itself; the noun from the same root, laid upon the Servant in Isaiah 53:6.
Hebrew chata' (H2398) — to miss the mark, to sin; the first verb of the threefold confession.
Hebrew rasha' (H7561) — to be wicked, to act wickedly; the third.
Hebrew 'iwweth (H5791) — to bend, to pervert; Psalm 119:78, they dealt perversely with me.
usage: “We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness” — three admissions.
“That which thy servant did perversely” — Shimei, when the wind had changed.
“They dealt perversely with me… but I will meditate in thy precepts”.

etymology: The Authorized Version's spelling of subtly, from Latin subtilis, finely woven — the image is of a thread so fine it is not seen. Related to the subtil serpent of Genesis 3:1, which is the standing biblical picture of the thing.
biblical_def: Stephen uses the word of the most consequential piece of state cunning in the Old Testament: Pharaoh “dealt subtilly with our kindred, and evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children, to the end they might not live” (Act 7:19). Exodus 1 shows the method — come on, let us deal wisely with them — taskmasters first, then a quiet word to the midwives, then at last the open command to drown the boys. Subtilty in Scripture is not an alternative to violence but its opening move. And the terrifying comment on it comes in the psalm: “He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal subtilly with his servants” (Psa 105:25). God is not the author of Pharaoh's sin, and Scripture never says He is; but the psalmist will not let the reader imagine that Egypt's cunning ran outside the government of God. The hardened heart served a purpose it did not intend. Saul uses the word of David, whom he was hunting: “it is told me that he dealeth very subtilly” (1Sa 23:22) — the pursuer projecting his own craft onto the man hiding in the wood. The serpent was subtil, Pharaoh dealt subtilly, and our Lord's instruction to His own is neither naive nor crafty: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subtile as thin, fine, delicate; and hence crafty, artful, cunning; subtly, as with artful cunning, or with nice discernment.
webster_full: SUBTILE, a. Thin; not dense or gross; as subtile air; subtile vapor.
1. Nice; fine; delicate; acute beyond ordinary perception.
2. Sly in design; artful; cunning; insinuating; as a subtile person.
SUBTILTY, n. Craftiness; cunning; artifice; the quality of being cunningly devised.
scriptures: Act 7:19
The same dealt subtilly with our kindred, and evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children, to the end they might not live.
He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal subtilly with his servants.
Go, I pray you, prepare yet, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who hath seen him there: for it is told me that he dealeth very subtilly.
corruption_summary: Cunning is admired as strategy; Scripture traces it to the serpent and shows where it ends.
corruption_paragraphs: Craft is one of the few vices the modern world honours outright: the shrewd operator, the clever manoeuvre, the man who plays the long game. Scripture credits the serpent with exactly this quality in the third verse of the third chapter of the Bible, and it has never been neutral since. Pharaoh's subtilty was applauded in Egypt as statecraft — let us deal wisely with them — and it produced a river full of drowned infants. The test is not intelligence, which Scripture prizes, but concealment of design: whether a man's aims can bear to be stated plainly to those they affect.

The pastoral corrective is our Lord's own, and it refuses both errors: wise as serpents, and harmless as doves (Mat 10:16). Believers are not commanded to be simple in the sense of gullible; the sheep among wolves needs to understand what wolves are. But the wisdom is put in harness with harmlessness, so that clear sight of the world's methods never becomes permission to use them. Paul's summary is the standard: we have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully (2Co 4:2).
roots_summary: Hebrew nakal (H5230), to act craftily, to deceive; 'arum (H6175), subtil, crafty — of the serpent; Greek katasophizomai (G2686), to outwit by sophistry.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakal (H5230) — to be crafty, to deal subtilly, to conspire; Psalm 105:25, Numbers 25:18.
Hebrew 'arum (H6175) — subtil, shrewd, crafty; Genesis 3:1, the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field.
Hebrew 'aram (H6191) — to be prudent or crafty; 1 Samuel 23:22, of David's supposed cunning.
Greek katasophizomai (G2686) — to deal craftily with, to outwit; Acts 7:19, of Pharaoh — the only New Testament occurrence.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — craftiness, readiness to do anything; 2 Corinthians 4:2, 11:3, lest your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
usage: “The same dealt subtilly with our kindred” — Stephen, on Pharaoh.
“He turned their heart… to deal subtilly with his servants”.
“He dealeth very subtilly” — Saul, describing himself.

pos: v. (the Authorized Version's spelling of loathe: to abhor, to turn from with disgust)
etymology: Saxon lathian, to be hateful. The seventeenth-century spelling drops the second a. Three of its four occurrences are Ezekiel's, and in every one of those the object of the loathing is the sinner's own self.
biblical_def: Ezekiel uses this word for something the modern church has almost entirely lost: the self-abhorrence that follows restoring grace. Not before it — after it. “And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives… and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations” (Eze 6:9). Again: “there shall ye remember your ways… and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed” (Eze 20:43). And most pointedly in the great new-covenant chapter, immediately after God promises the new heart, the new spirit and His own Spirit put within them: “Then shall ye remember your own evil ways… and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations” (Eze 36:31). The order is decisive. God cleanses, gives the new heart, causes them to walk in His statutes — and then they loathe themselves. This is not the despair of the unforgiven; it is the grief of the pardoned, and it deepens rather than diminishes as grace advances. The fourth occurrence is the plainest possible use: after the first plague “the Egyptians shall lothe to drink of the water of the river” (Exo 7:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loathe as to feel disgust at any thing; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to food or drink; and figuratively, to hate, to abhor.
webster_full: LOATHE, v.t. To feel disgust at any thing; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to food or drink.
1. To hate; to dislike greatly; to abhor. Ye shall loathe yourselves in your own sight. Ezekiel 20.
LOATHING, n. Extreme disgust; abhorrence.
ABHOR, v.t. To hate extremely, or with contempt; to loathe, detest or abominate.
scriptures: Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations.
And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed.
Eze 6:9

And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives, because I am broken with their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and with their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations.
Exo 7:18
And the fish that is in the river shall die, and the river shall stink; and the Egyptians shall lothe to drink of the water of the river.
corruption_summary: Self-loathing is treated as a pathology to be cured; Ezekiel makes it the fruit of the new heart, not its absence.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic reading of these verses is that they describe an unhealthy self-image, and the counsel given is to replace loathing with self-acceptance. Ezekiel 36 forbids the reading by its own sequence. God says He will sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, take away the stony heart, put His Spirit within them, cause them to walk in His statutes — and only then, then shall ye remember… and shall lothe yourselves. The abhorrence is the effect of grace already received. It is what a forgiven man feels when he sees, in the light of the mercy that saved him, what he actually was and did.

This must be distinguished with care from two counterfeits. It is not the despair of Judas, which had no hope in it and ended in a rope; godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation, and the sorrow of the world worketh death. And it is not the modern self-hatred that is really wounded pride, a man furious at himself for not being what he wished to be. Ezekiel's loathing is directed at sin against God, held by a man who knows he is pardoned, and it produces worship rather than paralysis. The Puritans knew this territory better than we do, and they were not morbid men; they were the freest.
roots_summary: Hebrew qut (H6962), to loathe, to feel a loathing at; la'ah (H3811), to be weary or disgusted; shiqquts (H8251), abomination, detestable thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew qut (H6962) — to loathe, to be grieved with, to feel a loathing; Ezekiel 6:9, 20:43, 36:31, always of loathing oneself.
Hebrew la'ah (H3811) — to be weary, to be disgusted with; Exodus 7:18, the Egyptians loathed to drink.
Hebrew to'ebah (H8441) — abomination, that which is detestable to God; the object of the loathing in Ezekiel 36:31.
Hebrew leb chadash (H3820, H2319) — a new heart; Ezekiel 36:26, given before the loathing of verse 31.
Greek metanoia (G3341) — a change of mind, repentance; 2 Corinthians 7:10, godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation.
usage: “Ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight” — after the new heart, not before.
“They shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed”.
“The Egyptians shall lothe to drink” — the plainest sense of the word.

pos: adj. and v. (loose, remiss, slow; to delay or let go)
etymology: Saxon slac, loose or remiss. The word runs through Scripture as the opposite of diligence and, in Peter's hands, becomes the answer to the oldest objection against the second coming.
biblical_def: “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2Pe 3:9). The scoffers had asked where the promise of His coming was, since all things continue as they were; Peter answers that the delay is not remissness but patience, and that the interval is mercy — time given for repentance. Read in its context the verse is not about God wishing to save every individual without exception while failing to do so; Peter is writing to the beloved, and the any and all are the us-ward he has just named, the elect for whose ingathering the world is still standing. The rest of the word's uses set the human standard. Vows: “thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21). Labour: “He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich” (Pro 10:4). Warfare: Gibeon's cry, “Slack not thy hand from thy servants; come up to us quickly” (Jos 10:6). Conquest: “How long are ye slack to go to possess the land, which the LORD God of your fathers hath given you?” (Jos 18:3). And judgment: He “will not be slack to him that hateth him” (Deu 7:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slack as not tense, loose; remiss, backward, not diligent; and slow, not quick or prompt.
webster_full: SLACK, a. Not tense; not hard drawn; not firmly extended; as a slack rope.
1. Weak; remiss; not holding fast; as a slack hand.
2. Slow; not prompt; tardy; as, to be slack in duty.
3. Not violent; not rapid; as a slack pace.
SLACKNESS, n. Remissness; negligence; inattention; want of eagerness.
scriptures: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
Jos 18:3
And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, How long are ye slack to go to possess the land, which the LORD God of your fathers hath given you?
When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee.
Pro 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
corruption_summary: God's patience is read as indifference or as universal salvation; Peter calls it longsuffering with an end in view.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors are built on 2 Peter 3:9. The scoffers Peter names draw one: the delay proves nothing is coming, since all things continue as they were from the beginning. Peter answers with the flood — the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished — and with the fire reserved for this one. The other error reads not willing that any should perish as a universal saving intention that fails, which would make God's purpose defeatable by the creature. Peter is writing to the beloved and speaks of longsuffering to us-ward; the delay is the gathering of the elect, and every day of it is mercy toward people not yet born.

The human side of the word deserves the sharper application. Joshua 18:3 was addressed to seven tribes who had won the land and had not gone in to take their portions — possessing what God had already given proved harder than fighting for it. That is a familiar shape. Believers who would face persecution bravely can spend years slack toward the promises actually held out to them: the mortification of a known sin, the family worship never begun, the vow made and not paid. Thou shalt not slack to pay it is written to such men.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'achar (H309), to delay, to be slack; raphah (H7503), to sink, relax, let drop; Greek braduno (G1019), to be slow or tardy.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'achar (H309) — to delay, to tarry; Deuteronomy 23:21, thou shalt not slack to pay thy vow.
Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to sink down, to relax, to let go; Joshua 10:6 (slack not thy hand), Zephaniah 3:16.
Hebrew remiyyah (H7423) — slackness, deceit, negligence; Proverbs 10:4, a slack hand — the same word rendered deceitful elsewhere.
Greek braduno (G1019) — to be slow, to delay; 2 Peter 3:9, 1 Timothy 3:15.
Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be longsuffering, patient of spirit; the word Peter sets against slackness.
usage: “The Lord is not slack… but is longsuffering” — the delay is the mercy.
“How long are ye slack to go to possess the land” — seven tribes, already victorious.
“He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand”.

pos: n. (dread; the state of being seized with terror)
etymology: From fearful and the noun ending -ness. In the Authorized Version the word never means reverence; it is always the dread that overtakes a man against his will, and it is used of a psalmist, a prophet, and the hypocrites in Zion.
biblical_def: This is dread, not reverence, and Scripture distributes it carefully. David: “Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me” (Psa 55:5) — the psalm of the friend's betrayal, where the terror is not of an enemy but of a familiar friend who went with him to the house of God in company. Isaiah, given the vision of Babylon's fall: “My heart panted, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me” (Isa 21:4). A true prophet is not exhilarated by a vision of judgment; it makes him sick. And then the verse that governs the word: “The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” (Isa 33:14). The hypocrites are in Zion — inside the church, in the congregation, at the ordinances — and what surprises them is the discovery that the God they had been near is a consuming fire. Isaiah answers his own question in the next verse: he that walketh righteously and speaketh uprightly shall dwell on high. The same fire that terrifies the hypocrite is the dwelling of the righteous, and the difference is not the fire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fearfulness as timorousness; state of being afraid; and fearful as affected by fear, apprehensive, or terrible to behold.
webster_full: FEARFULNESS, n. Timorousness; timidity.
1. State of being afraid; awe; dread.
FEARFUL, a. Affected by fear; feeling pain in expectation of evil; apprehensive with solicitude.
1. Terrible; impressing fear; frightful; dreadful. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
scriptures: The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?
Psa 55:5
Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me.
Isa 21:4
My heart panted, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me.
corruption_summary: Fear of judgment is treated as a manipulation the church should abandon; Isaiah puts it inside Zion and calls it a surprise.
corruption_paragraphs: It is now widely held that preaching which produces dread is a failure of the gospel — emotional coercion, unworthy of a God of love. Isaiah 33:14 describes something the modern pulpit rarely produces: fearfulness surprising the hypocrites in Zion, people already inside the congregation discovering that the holiness they had been treating as a comfortable atmosphere is a devouring fire. Our Lord Himself said, fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. A ministry that has removed this category has not made God safer; it has left the hypocrite undisturbed until the day when the discovery cannot be acted upon.

But Scripture does not leave the believer in dread, and this is where the doctrine must be held whole. The same prophet answers his own question immediately, and the New Testament answers it finally: there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, and perfect love casteth out fear. The everlasting burnings are the presence of God, which is torment to the unreconciled and home to the redeemed. Fearfulness is the right response to that presence for a man out of Christ, and it is meant to drive him to Christ, where it becomes reverence and ceases to be terror.
roots_summary: Hebrew yir'ah (H3374), fear, dread, reverence; pallatsuth (H6427), shuddering, horror; chaneph (H2611), profane, hypocrite.
roots_lines: Hebrew yir'ah (H3374) — fear, terror, and in other contexts reverence; Psalm 55:5, Isaiah 21:4.
Hebrew pallatsuth (H6427) — shuddering, trembling horror; Isaiah 21:4, Job 21:6, Ezekiel 7:18.
Hebrew ra'ad (H7461) — trembling; Psalm 55:5, fearfulness and trembling.
Hebrew chaneph (H2611) — profane, godless, hypocrite; Isaiah 33:14, whom the fearfulness surprised.
Greek phoberos (G5398) — fearful, terrible; Hebrews 10:31, it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
usage: “Fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites” — and they were in Zion.
“Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me” — a friend had betrayed him.
“The night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear” — a prophet sickened by his own vision.

pos: n. (levity; want of weight or seriousness; inconstancy)
etymology: From light in the sense of not heavy, Saxon leoht. Scripture's moral use is the opposite of glory, whose Hebrew root means weight: a light man is one whose word and conduct carry no mass.
biblical_def: Three occurrences, and each names a different failure of weight. Jeremiah of the nation: “it came to pass through the lightness of her whoredom, that she defiled the land, and committed adultery with stones and with stocks” (Jer 3:9) — the sin was not merely committed but committed lightly, without gravity, which is what made it possible to do it at all. Then of the false prophets: “I am against them that prophesy false dreams… and cause my people to err by their lies, and by their lightness; yet I sent them not, nor commanded them: therefore they shall not profit this people at all” (Jer 23:32). Lightness is here a professional vice of preachers — not chiefly falsehood but frivolity, a man handling the word of God without weight, and God's verdict is that such men shall not profit this people at all. Paul uses it of himself in self-defence: “When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay?” (2Co 1:17). He had changed a travel plan and was accused of being a man whose word meant nothing, and he answers by pointing to the God whose promises in Christ are yea and amen. A Christian's reliability is a theological matter, because he represents a God who does not say yes and no.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lightness as want of weight; and figuratively, levity, inconstancy, unsteadiness, want of due consideration.
webster_full: LIGHTNESS, n. Want of weight; levity; the contrary to heaviness.
1. Inconstancy; unsteadiness; the quality of mind which disposes it to be influenced by trifling considerations.
2. Levity; want of due consideration; frivolity.
3. Agility; nimbleness.
scriptures: Behold, I am against them that prophesy false dreams, saith the LORD, and do tell them, and cause my people to err by their lies, and by their lightness; yet I sent them not, nor commanded them: therefore they shall not profit this people at all, saith the LORD.
When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay?
Jer 3:9
And it came to pass through the lightness of her whoredom, that she defiled the land, and committed adultery with stones and with stocks.
corruption_summary: Levity in the pulpit is prized as accessibility; Jeremiah lists lightness beside lies as a reason prophets profit nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 23:32 puts two things in one indictment: by their lies, and by their lightness. We are practised at examining the first and almost blind to the second. A man may say nothing false and still handle the word of God with a levity that empties it — the joke that dissolves the weight of a text, the constant self-deprecation that keeps everything at room temperature, the studied casualness that assures a congregation nothing here is heavy enough to require anything of them. The Lord's verdict is not that such preaching is less effective. It is that they shall not profit this people at all.

This is not a call for gloom, and the Puritans, who are usually libelled on this point, were not gloomy men; the same tradition that produced Owen on mortification produced Rutherford's letters and Watson's wit. Gravity in Scripture is not the absence of joy but the presence of weight — the Hebrew for glory means heaviness. And Paul's use adds the ordinary form of the duty: keep your word. A believer whose commitments are provisional, whose yes needs qualifying, has been light in the sense the Bible most often means, and it dishonours the God in whom all the promises are yea and amen.
roots_summary: Hebrew qol / qalal (H7043), to be light, slight, of small account; pachazuth (H6350), frivolity, wantonness; Greek elaphria (G1644), levity, fickleness.
roots_lines: Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, trifling, of small account; Jeremiah 3:9, the lightness of her whoredom.
Hebrew pachazuth (H6350) — frivolity, recklessness, wantonness; Jeremiah 23:32, the prophets' lightness.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, literally weight; the exact opposite of lightness, and the standard by which it is judged.
Greek elaphria (G1644) — levity, fickleness, lightness; 2 Corinthians 1:17, the only New Testament occurrence.
Greek nai kai amen (G3483, G281) — yea and amen; 2 Corinthians 1:20, all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen.
usage: “By their lies, and by their lightness” — two counts, one indictment.
“Did I use lightness?” — Paul, answering for a changed travel plan.
“Through the lightness of her whoredom” — sin made possible by being taken lightly.

pos: adj. (not believing; without faith; of a spouse, a Jew, a defiled conscience, and the damned)
etymology: From un- and believing. The New Testament word is apistos — literally faithless — and it functions as a settled category rather than a description of a mood: a man is either in the faith or he is not.
biblical_def: Paul's hardest pastoral case uses this word twice in two verses. To believers married to unconverted spouses: “the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy” (1Co 7:14). The sanctification here is not salvation — Paul asks two verses later how the believing spouse knows whether the other will be saved — but a covenantal setting-apart: the household stands under the gospel's influence rather than being defiled by the unbeliever's presence, and the children have a place in it. Hence the rule: do not leave. And the corresponding rule if the unbeliever leaves: “if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace” (1Co 7:15). Titus gives the moral effect of unbelief: “Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled” (Tit 1:15) — the problem is not the object but the eye. And Revelation puts the word in the most sobering list in Scripture: “the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers… shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone” (Rev 21:8). Unbelief stands second, before murder.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unbelieving as not believing, withholding belief, or infidel — and specifically, not believing the divine revelation.
webster_full: UNBELIEVING, a. Not believing; withholding belief, particularly in divine revelation.
1. Infidel; not believing the truths of the gospel.
UNBELIEF, n. Incredulity; the withholding of belief; particularly, disbelief of divine revelation, or the doctrines of Christianity.
INFIDEL, n. One who disbelieves and rejects Christianity.
scriptures: For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy.
But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
Tit 1:15
Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled.
corruption_summary: Unbelief is treated as a neutral intellectual position; Revelation lists it among the sins that end in the second death.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern mind classes unbelief as a lack — the absence of a conviction, morally weightless, a matter of evidence and temperament. Scripture classes it as a sin, and Revelation 21:8 sets it second in a list that runs on to murderers and idolaters. The reason is that unbelief is not primarily an intellectual verdict but a refusal of testimony: he that believeth not God hath made him a liar (1Jo 5:10). John 3 says the condemnation is that light is come into the world and men loved darkness rather than light. That is a moral account of unbelief, and it is the Bible's.

The pastoral half of the word must be handled with equal care, because 1 Corinthians 7 is constantly misused in both directions. It does not teach that a believing spouse saves the other — Paul explicitly leaves that open. And it does not license a believer to leave an unconverted husband or wife: let him not put her away. What it grants is peace when the unbeliever departs, and hope while he stays. Peter adds the method for the wife in that house: without the word, won by the conversation of the wives (1Pe 3:1-2). Long obedience, not argument, is the instrument God most often uses there.
roots_summary: Greek apistos (G571), without faith, unbelieving, faithless; apeitheo (G544), to refuse to be persuaded; hagiazo (G37), to set apart, sanctify.
roots_lines: Greek apistos (G571) — unbelieving, faithless, an unbeliever; 1 Corinthians 7:14-15, Titus 1:15, Revelation 21:8.
Greek hagiazo (G37) — to set apart, to sanctify; 1 Corinthians 7:14, of the unbelieving spouse set apart by the believing one.
Greek douloo (G1402) — to enslave, to bring into bondage; 1 Corinthians 7:15, the believer is not under bondage.
Greek apeitheo (G544) — to be disobedient, to refuse belief; John 3:36, he that believeth not the Son shall not see life.
Greek deuteros thanatos (G1208, G2288) — the second death; Revelation 20:14, 21:8.
usage: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife” — set apart, not saved.
“If the unbelieving depart, let him depart” — and God hath called us to peace.
“The fearful, and unbelieving” — second in the list, before murderers.

pos: adj. (raging; full of fury; of angry men, of a heathen king, and of the LORD's rebukes)
etymology: Latin furiosus, from furere, to rage. Scripture applies the word both to men who cannot govern their anger and to God, whose fury is never ungoverned — and the entry turns on holding that difference.
biblical_def: Proverbs treats the furious man as a contagion to be avoided: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go” (Pro 22:24) — and the next verse gives the reason, lest thou learn his ways and get a snare to thy soul. Temper is caught. “An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression” (Pro 29:22): the wrath does not stay one sin but multiplies into many. Daniel shows a furious king: Nebuchadnezzar “was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon” (Dan 2:12) — a whole class of men sentenced because the king could not recover his dream, which is the natural end of unrestrained power joined to unrestrained temper. Then the harder half of the word. Nahum opens: “God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies” (Nah 1:2). Ezekiel speaks twice of “furious rebukes” (Eze 5:15; 25:17). The wrath of God is not a lapse of self-command; it is His settled and holy opposition to evil, measured, announced beforehand by prophets, and — in the same book — joined to this: the LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines furious as raging, violent, transported with passion; and fury as a storm of anger, madness, rage.
webster_full: FURIOUS, a. Rushing with impetuosity; moving with violence; as a furious stream.
1. Raging; violent; transported with passion; as a furious animal.
2. Mad; frantic.
FURY, n. A storm of anger; madness; rage; a violent passion.
1. Enthusiasm; heat of the mind.
scriptures: Nah 1:2
God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies.
Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go:
An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression.
Dan 2:12
For this cause the king was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.
corruption_summary: Divine wrath is denied as unworthy of God; Nahum opens his prophecy with it and closes the chapter with God's goodness.
corruption_paragraphs: It is now common, and not only among liberal theologians, to treat the wrath of God as an Old Testament embarrassment or as a mere metaphor for the impersonal consequences of sin. Nahum 1:2 does not permit it, nor does the New Testament, where the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness (Rom 1:18) and the Lamb Himself has wrath (Rev 6:16). The doctrine matters because the cross depends on it: if there is no wrath, the propitiation is theatre. Penal substitution means that the fury which Nahum announces fell somewhere, and the gospel is that it fell on Christ in the place of His people.

Holding that, the distinction from human fury must be kept sharp. God's is holy, informed, proportioned and announced in advance by prophets who were sent for years to warn; man's is the loss of self-government that Proverbs says multiplies transgression and that James says worketh not the righteousness of God. The believer who defends divine wrath while excusing his own temper has misunderstood both. Be ye angry, and sin not is possible only for the man who has ceased to enjoy his anger.
roots_summary: Hebrew chemah (H2534), heat, fury, wrath; ba'al chemah, a master of fury — the furious man; Aramaic qetsaph (H7108), to be enraged.
roots_lines: Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, burning anger, fury; Nahum 1:2, Ezekiel 5:15, and in the phrase ba'al chemah, a master of wrath (Proverbs 22:24, 29:22).
Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; Nahum 1:2, three times in one verse.
Hebrew qanno' (H7072) — jealous; the first word of Nahum's description, and the ground of the rest.
Aramaic qetsaph (H7108) — to be enraged; Daniel 2:12, of Nebuchadnezzar.
Greek orge (G3709) — settled indignation, wrath; Romans 1:18, 5:9, John 3:36 — the wrath of God abideth on him.
usage: “The LORD revengeth, and is furious” — and the same chapter says He is good.
“With a furious man thou shalt not go” — lest thou learn his ways.
“Angry and very furious” — and a whole college of wise men sentenced.
